ports.name: Bear Harbor Landing
ports.county: Mendocino (northernmost Mendocino, functionally Lost Coast / southern Humboldt trade)
ports.active_years: 1874-1907 (NR period of significance; first documented vessel shipment Dec 1874 sloop Mayflower; landing/chute built 1884-85; last known product shipment 1907; 1915 pier-rebuild notice with no evidence of reopening)
ports.heyday: 1898-1902 under Bear Harbor Lumber Co.; 112+ cargoes 1892-1899, peaking at 29 trips in 1899
ports.loading_method: Two successive hybrid pier+chute systems: (1) 1885 pier off Morgan Rock with trough-chute apron arm at its end (Peterson 1885 survey; Davidson 1889 describes wharf 'with an apron over fifteen feet of water'); (2) June 1890, new 300-ft pier at Cluster Cone Rocks with WIRE chute at its end ('similar to the one at Noyo Landing'), extended 100 ft in 1892 and again ~1895/1898; SF Chronicle 16 Jan 1898: wharf 250 ft through rocks, wire runs 420 ft to the vessel ~40 ft above water. Donkey engine powered the wire (a spark from the chute's donkey engine burned 400 ft of pier 8 Apr 1903). 1901 rebuild put on 1,500 ties/hour, 'fastest work ever done over a wire chute in Mendocino County' (Ukiah Dispatch 15 Nov 1901)
ports.wharf: yes - pier (not a true wharf per NR nomination terminology); 550-600 ft after all extensions; destroyed by 14-ft 'tidal wave' 21 Nov 1899 (2 killed, incl. near-miss of company president Calvin Stewart), rebuilt 1901; burned in part 1903; destroyed again by storms Christmas 1905; partially rebuilt 1906-07
ports.size_category: doghole-with-wharf; 15 ft water at pier end at low tide; vessels to ~200 tons under the chute (Peterson 1885), room for 3-4 vessels moored in summer; two-masted schooners (Georgia R. ports.summary: The definitive Lost Coast doghole port: split-products (above all tanbark) exported by schooner from 1874 and by steam schooner from 1890 over two successive pier-and-chute systems, fed after 1893 by the Bear Harbor & Eel River Railroad with its 2,000-ft gravity incline over the coastal ridge. The Southern Humboldt Lumber Co.'s half-million-dollar Andersonia sawmill was finished in 1905 but destroyed by the 18 April 1906 earthquake before ever cutting lumber; the port shipped its last products in 1907. 46+ vessels carried cargoes to 14 California ports over 33 years.
ports.confidence_notes: Exceptionally well documented (2022-23 NR nomination with newspaper-level citations). Discrepancies flagged: incline length 1,900 vs 2,000 ft; 3 vs 4 rails at incline midpoint; railway gauge (standard vs narrow) unresolved; MPDF gives McCornack sale as 1893 but the fuller NR nomination documents Nov 1889 sale to Weller & Stewart. Davidson 1889 says wharf built 1885, NR gives open-for-business 4 July 1885.

ports.summary: The northernmost Mendocino doghole port, half-way between Bear Harbor and Shelter Cove. A wire-chute pier reputedly the highest and longest on the Mendocino coast shipped railroad ties, tanbark, and Whitethorn Valley shingles from the 1890s; a 3-mile railway (1890, Stetson) linked mill and landing. Chute operated until about 1930, making it one of the longest-lived Lost Coast landings.

ports.summary: The only semi-sheltered roadstead on the Lost Coast (Davidson 1889 describes it as the standard summer refuge). A 960-ft pier of 1885 served the southern Humboldt backcountry - tanbark, wool, hides, butter out; supplies in - by mule train and later wagon road. Its timber-products traffic was captured by Bear Harbor and Needle Rock in the 1890s, and the pier decayed until maintenance was abandoned in the 1930s; salmon fishing then rum-running sustained the place.

ports.name: Eureka (Humboldt Bay) - the deepwater lumber capital
alt_names: Humboldt Bay; Tebenkov's 'Bay of Indians'/'entrance of Rezanoff' (1848 atlas); Indian name Qual-a-waloo (Davidson 1869)

No less than eight railroads... are built from various points on the shores of Humboldt Bay' - Davidson 1889); post-1906-earthquake boom; after Oct 1914 the NWP railroad progressively replaced steam schooners as the main outlet
ports.loading_method: Wharves along the Eureka waterfront - 'Vessels lie at the wharves to load lumber and produce, and rest on the mud at low-tide' (Davidson 1889); mill-side wharves on Indian/Gunther Island ('extensive saw-mill buildings and wharves,' 1889); channel to Eureka dredged by U.S. Engineers (1889). BAR SYSTEM: shifting bar with 13-25 ft; steam tug stationed on the bar from c.1852 - flag hoisted on Red Bluff, tug goes out, 'The best advice we can offer in regard to entering the bay is to wait for the tug' (Davidson 1869); pilots' flagstaff ranges on Red Bluff; lumber-laden vessels detained up to 25-31 days in bad weather (1851, 1861); can-buoy moorings outside (1869). ports.summary: California's redwood metropolis: nine mills on the bay by 1854, the first redwood cargo 1855, and by 1889 'the great lumber center of this region' with enormous shipping, direct foreign trade, and eight feeder railroads (Davidson). Its notorious shifting bar bred the earliest tug-assisted bar-crossing system on the coast (c.1852) and, from 1889-91, federal jetties. John Dolbeer's donkey engine (Eureka, Aug 1881) mechanized West Coast logging from here. The NWP's completion (23 Oct 1914) turned the lumber flow from sea to rail, though steam schooners persisted into the 1920s-30s.
